# Figure helper: includes res_dir/file if it exists, otherwise a labelled
# placeholder float, so that \ref{fig:<label>} always resolves and knitting
# never fails because of missing experiment output.
todo_fig <- function(file, caption, label, what, width = 0.85) {
  path <- file.path(res_dir, file)
  ok <- file.exists(path)
  if (!ok) caption <- paste("[Placeholder]", caption)
  cat("\n\\begin{figure}[htbp]\n\\centering\n")
  if (ok) {
    cat(sprintf("\\includegraphics[width=%.2f\\linewidth]{%s}\n", width, path))
  } else {
    cat(sprintf(paste0(
      "\\fcolorbox{orange}{yellow!8}{\\parbox{0.88\\linewidth}{\\small",
      "\\textbf{Figure placeholder.} %s \\textit{Expected file:} \\texttt{%s}}}\n"),
      tex_esc(what), tex_esc(path)))
  }
  cat(sprintf("\\caption{%s}\n\\label{fig:%s}\n\\end{figure}\n\n", caption, label))
  invisible(ok)
}

# Table helper: renders res_dir/file (CSV) with kable if it exists and is
# non-empty, otherwise a labelled placeholder table float.
todo_tab <- function(file, caption, label, what) {
  path <- file.path(res_dir, file)
  df <- NULL
  if (file.exists(path)) {
    df <- tryCatch(utils::read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
                   error = function(e) NULL)
  }
  if (!is.null(df) && nrow(df) > 0) {
    cat("\n\\begingroup\\small\n")
    cat(knitr::kable(df, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, caption = caption,
                     label = label, digits = 4, linesep = ""), sep = "\n")
    cat("\n\\endgroup\n\n")
  } else {
    cat("\n\\begin{table}[htbp]\n\\centering\n")
    cat(sprintf("\\caption{[Placeholder] %s}\n\\label{tab:%s}\n", caption, label))

      "\\textbf{Table placeholder.} %s \\textit{Expected file:} \\texttt{%s}}}\n"),
      tex_esc(what), tex_esc(path)))
    cat("\\end{table}\n\n")
  }
  invisible(NULL)
}

# Introduction {#ch:intro}

## Motivation

Many systems need to know *how many different* items they have seen, not how many items they have seen in total: distinct source addresses in network traffic, distinct visitors or queries in a log, distinct values of an attribute in a database column. Such counts are used for monitoring, anomaly detection and query planning \cite{fm,lru,muthu}. When the data arrive as a very long stream, or are spread over many machines, keeping a record of every item already seen can be unaffordable. Distinct-element estimation asks how much accuracy must be given up to avoid this cost.

\begin{todobox}
Add one or two concrete motivating scenarios that the team can substantiate with a citation (for example from \cite{lru} or \cite{muthu}) or leave generic. Avoid unsupported statements about industrial usage.
\end{todobox}

## Problem statement

Given a stream $\sigma=(a_1,\dots,a_m)$ over a universe $[n]$, output an estimate $\dhat$ of the number $d=\Fzero(\sigma)$ of distinct items, using memory far smaller than $d$, in a single pass, with relative error at most $\eps$ except with probability at most $\delta$. The formal definitions are given in Chapter \ref{ch:foundations}; they are deliberately not repeated here.

## Why exact counting is expensive in a stream

An exact algorithm must in effect remember which items have appeared, so its memory grows linearly with $d$ in the worst case (Section \ref{sec:exact}). For streams with hundreds of millions of distinct items this is the bottleneck that motivates sublinear-space randomized estimators.

## Objectives and scope

The project (i) explains the mathematical basis of BJKST, (ii) implements the algorithm from first principles, (iii) evaluates its accuracy and efficiency experimentally against exact counting, (iv) studies its behaviour under several stream distributions, and (v) provides an interactive demonstration. A comparison with HyperLogLog is an optional extension.

\begin{todobox}
State precisely what is in scope: programming language, maximum stream length and universe size tested, which BJKST forms are implemented (identifier-storing and/or fingerprint form, Section \ref{sec:space}), and whether the median amplification (Section \ref{sec:median}) is implemented. State what is explicitly out of scope (for instance, distributed or sliding-window variants).
\end{todobox}

## Core research question and research questions

**Core question.** To what extent do the theoretical guarantees of the BJKST estimator predict its measured accuracy, memory and running time, and under which conditions is approximate counting preferable to exact counting?

This is refined into six research questions, each of which is revisited in Chapter \ref{ch:discussion}.

\begin{description}
\item[RQ1 (accuracy).] How does the relative error depend on $\eps$ and on the true cardinality $d$, and is the empirical failure frequency consistent with the single-copy guarantee of Theorem \ref{thm:accuracy}, provided the implementation satisfies the theorem's assumptions?
\item[RQ2 (memory).] How do the buffer size and measured peak memory scale with $\eps$ and $d$, compared with the exact hash set?
\item[RQ3 (runtime).] How does the per-item cost scale with stream length, and what is the overhead of hashing and pruning relative to exact counting?
\item[RQ4 (distribution sensitivity).] Does behaviour differ across uniform, high-duplication, high-cardinality and skewed streams, as the analysis (which depends only on the set of distinct items) predicts?
\item[RQ5 (randomness).] How large is the run-to-run variability across random seeds, how do the tails look, and what does median amplification change?
\item[RQ6 (hashing).] How do practical hash functions compare with the pairwise independent family assumed by the analysis?
\end{description}

# Problem Formulation and Mathematical Foundations {#ch:foundations}

This chapter fixes the problem and collects only the tools used in the analysis of Chapter \ref{ch:bjkst}: Chebyshev's inequality for the accuracy of one copy, Hoeffding's inequality for amplification, and pairwise independent hashing with trailing zeros for the sampling mechanism. Standard material is stated without proof and referenced to \cite{mu,mr}. This chapter follows WP1, Sections 2--4.

## The streaming model

Let $[n]=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ be the universe. A *stream* is a sequence $\sigma=(a_1,\dots,a_m)$ with $a_t\in[n]$, presented one item at a time. A streaming algorithm makes a single pass over $\sigma$ (in the basic model), uses memory sublinear in $m$ and $n$ (ideally polylogarithmic, or polynomial in $1/\eps$ times polylogarithmic), and spends little time per item. The cost measure is the number of bits of working memory \cite{ams,muthu}. Without loss of generality $n=2^b$ is a power of two (pad the universe otherwise). The input is arbitrary but fixed in advance; all probabilities are over the algorithm's internal randomness.

## Distinct elements and the cost of exact counting {#sec:exact}

Let $f_i=|\{t:a_t=i\}|$ be the frequency of $i\in[n]$. The $k$-th frequency moment is $F_k=\sum_{i\in[n]}f_i^k$ with $0^0=0$ \cite{ams}; $F_1=m$ is the stream length, and
$$\Fzero \;=\; \bigl|\{i: f_i>0\}\bigr| \;=:\; d$$
is the number of distinct elements. Write $D\subseteq[n]$ for the set of distinct items, so $|D|=d$.

Computing $d$ exactly requires $\Omega(\min\{n,m\})$ bits in the worst case, since the algorithm must essentially remember which items have occurred. WP1 also states that the same $\Omega(n)$ barrier holds for \emph{deterministic} algorithms that merely approximate $\Fzero$ within a fixed constant factor, attributing this to \cite{ams}. Hence both randomization and approximation are needed for polylogarithmic space.

\begin{authornote}
WP1, Section 2.3: the precise statement of the deterministic-approximation lower bound attributed to Alon--Matias--Szegedy should be checked against \cite{ams} before it is quoted in the final report (exact approximation factor and quantifiers). The exact-counting bound is standard but is stated without proof in WP1.
\end{authornote}

## Approximation guarantee

\begin{definition}[$(\eps,\delta)$-approximation]\label{def:approx}
A randomized algorithm outputs an $(\eps,\delta)$-approximation of $d$ if its output $\dhat$ satisfies $\Prb\bigl[\,|\dhat-d|\le\eps d\,\bigr]\ge 1-\delta$, where the probability is over the algorithm's internal randomness, not over the input.
\end{definition}

## Probabilistic tools

\begin{lemma}[Chebyshev]\label{lem:cheb}
For any random variable $X$ with finite variance and any $t>0$, $\Prb[\,|X-\E X|\ge t\,]\le \Var[X]/t^2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Variance of a pairwise independent sum]\label{lem:var}
If $X_1,\dots,X_d$ are pairwise independent, then $\Var\bigl[\sum_i X_i\bigr]=\sum_i \Var[X_i]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$\Var[\sum_i X_i]=\sum_i\Var[X_i]+\sum_{i\neq j}\mathrm{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$, and pairwise independence gives $\mathrm{Cov}(X_i,X_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Hoeffding]\label{lem:hoeff}
Let $W_1,\dots,W_k$ be independent $\{0,1\}$-valued random variables and $W=\sum_j W_j$. Then for every $t>0$, $\Prb[W-\E W\ge t]\le \exp(-2t^2/k)$.
\end{lemma}

Only the second moment (Chebyshev with Lemma \ref{lem:var}) is needed to analyse a single copy of BJKST; Hoeffding is used solely for amplification (Section \ref{sec:median}). Markov's inequality, which underlies Chebyshev, is not restated; see \cite{mu,mr}.

## Hash functions

Let $\mathcal H$ be a family of functions $h:U\to R$, with $h$ drawn uniformly from $\mathcal H$.

\begin{definition}[Pairwise independent family]\label{def:pairwise}
$\mathcal H$ is \emph{pairwise independent} (``strongly 2-universal'' in the Carter--Wegman terminology) if for all distinct $x,y\in U$ and all $r,s\in R$, $\Prb_{h\in\mathcal H}[h(x)=r\wedge h(y)=s]=1/|R|^2$. Equivalently, each $h(x)$ is uniform on $R$ and, for distinct $x,y$, the values $h(x),h(y)$ are independent.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[2-universal family]\label{def:universal}
$\mathcal H$ is \emph{2-universal} if $\Prb_{h\in\mathcal H}[h(x)=h(y)]\le 1/|R|$ for all distinct $x,y\in U$.
\end{definition}

Pairwise independence implies 2-universality \cite{cw,wc}; see also \cite{clrs}. The converse fails: the single identity map $h(x)=x$ on $R=U$ is 2-universal (it never collides) but is deterministic, hence not pairwise independent. The two notions must not be conflated: the analysis below uses a \emph{pairwise independent} $h$ for sampling (variance additivity, Lemma \ref{lem:var}) and only a \emph{2-universal} $g$ for fingerprints (union bound over collisions, Theorem \ref{thm:fingerprint}).

### An explicit pairwise independent family {-}

Let $F=\mathrm{GF}(2^b)$, whose elements are identified with $b$-bit strings and hence with $[n]$ when $n=2^b$. Define $\mathcal H=\{h_{a,c}:F\to F,\ h_{a,c}(x)=a\cdot x+c\ :\ a,c\in F\}$.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:gf}
$\mathcal H$ is a pairwise independent family of functions $[n]\to[n]$. Choosing $h\in\mathcal H$ requires $2b=2\log_2 n$ random bits, which is also its description length.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Fix distinct $x,y\in F$ and targets $r,s\in F$. The system $ax+c=r$, $ay+c=s$ has the unique solution $a=(r-s)/(x-y)$, $c=r-ax$, because $x-y\neq0$ is invertible in a field. Exactly one of the $|F|^2=n^2$ pairs $(a,c)$ realises $(h(x),h(y))=(r,s)$, so the probability is $1/n^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Over a prime field $\mathbb Z_p$ the map $x\mapsto ax+c \bmod p$ is also pairwise independent into $\mathbb Z_p$, but the range is then not a power of two and the trailing-zero events below have probability only approximately $2^{-z}$. Using $\mathrm{GF}(2^b)$ makes the probabilities exact. (This matters for implementation: see Section \ref{sec:hashing-design}.)
\end{remark}

### Trailing zeros {-}

For $x\in\{0,\dots,2^b-1\}$ let $\zeros(x)$ be the number of trailing zeros of its $b$-bit binary expansion, with $\zeros(0)=b$.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:tz}
If $X$ is uniform on $\{0,\dots,2^b-1\}$, then for every integer $0\le z\le b$, $\Prb[\zeros(X)\ge z]=2^{-z}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$\zeros(X)\ge z$ iff the lowest $z$ bits of $X$ are zero, i.e.\ $2^z\mid X$; exactly $2^{b-z}$ of the $2^b$ values are multiples of $2^z$.
\end{proof}

# BJKST Algorithm and Theoretical Analysis {#ch:bjkst}

This chapter follows WP1, Sections 5--10, and is the mathematical core of the report. All results in it are \evid{Literature}: a re-derivation of results from \cite{bjkst} (primary source), with the buffer-with-threshold presentation in the style of \cite{chak}. Nothing here is claimed to be new.

## Intuition

Hash every item to a $b$-bit value. If $h$ behaves uniformly, the fraction of distinct items whose hash has at least $z$ trailing zeros is $2^{-z}$. Keeping only those items gives a small random sample of the distinct items; multiplying the sample size by $2^z$ rescales it to an estimate of $d$. Because retention depends on the \emph{value} of an item and not on the position of its occurrences, duplicates cannot change the sample, which is why the sampled quantity counts \emph{distinct} elements. The remaining difficulty is that the right level $z$ depends on the unknown $d$; BJKST finds it on the fly by raising $z$ whenever the sample exceeds a threshold.

## The variant analysed and its assumptions {#sec:variant}

The original paper presents three algorithms \cite{bjkst}. The variant analysed here is the **buffer-with-threshold sampling formulation**, first in an *identifier-storing form* (Algorithm \ref{alg:bjkst}) and then in a *fingerprint form* (Section \ref{sec:space}). Its analysis assumes:

\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textbf{A1}] One pass; the stream is arbitrary but fixed in advance (non-adaptive input).
\item[\textbf{A2}] The universe is $[n]$ with $n=2^b$.
\item[\textbf{A3}] $h:[n]\to[n]$ is drawn uniformly from the $\mathrm{GF}(2^b)$ affine family of Lemma \ref{lem:gf}; only its pairwise independence is used.
\item[\textbf{A4}] In the fingerprint form, $g:[n]\to[M]$ is 2-universal and independent of $h$.
\item[\textbf{A5}] The threshold is $\tau=\lceil c/\eps^2\rceil$ with $c=60$, and $0<\eps<1$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{authornote}
WP1 states that the formulation ``follows the style of lecture-note treatments, e.g.\ \cite{chak}'' and that \cite{bjkst} presents three algorithms. Which of the three algorithms in \cite{bjkst} (if any) coincides with Algorithm \ref{alg:bjkst}, and whether the constant $c=60$ and the choice $M=\lceil10\tau^2(b+1)^2\rceil$ come from a source or are WP1's own choices, are not stated. Confirm and cite precisely, or describe them as ``derived in WP1''. The report should not say ``the original BJKST algorithm'' without this check.
\end{authornote}

## Hash-based sampling and nested samples

Fix $h$ as in A3. For each level $z\in\{0,\dots,b\}$ define the level-$z$ sample and its size
$$S_z=\{a\in D:\ \zeros(h(a))\ge z\},\qquad Y_z=|S_z|.$$

\begin{proposition}[Properties of the level-$z$ sample]\label{prop:sample}
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every $a\in D$ and $0\le z\le b$, $\Prb[a\in S_z]=2^{-z}$ exactly.
\item For distinct $a\ne a'$ the events $\{a\in S_z\}$ and $\{a'\in S_z\}$ are independent.
\item $D=S_0\supseteq S_1\supseteq S_2\supseteq\cdots$, deterministically.
\item Membership of $a$ in $S_z$ is a function of $a$ and $h$ only; hence an item occurring $f_a$ times is retained at all of its occurrences or at none.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(1) $h(a)$ is uniform on $[n]$ (Lemma \ref{lem:gf}), so Lemma \ref{lem:tz} applies. (2) $h(a),h(a')$ are independent, and the events are functions of them. (3) $\zeros(h(a))\ge z+1\Rightarrow\zeros(h(a))\ge z$. (4) is immediate from the definition.
\end{proof}

The nesting in (3) is what allows the algorithm to tighten its sample without re-reading the stream: the level-$(z+1)$ sample is obtained from the level-$z$ sample by discarding the items whose stored value $\zeros(h(a))$ equals exactly $z$.

\begin{authornote}
WP1 additionally says that each item survives from level $z$ to $z+1$ ``independently, in the pairwise sense, with conditional probability $1/2$''. This sentence is informal and is not used in any proof (only the deterministic nesting (3) is). It is omitted here; restore it only with a precise statement.
\end{authornote}

## The estimator

Define $\dhat_z=2^zY_z$.

\begin{proposition}[Mean and variance at a fixed level]\label{prop:var}
For every $0\le z\le b$, with $\mu_z:=\E[Y_z]=d/2^z$,
$$\E[\dhat_z]=d,\qquad \Var[Y_z]=d\,2^{-z}(1-2^{-z})\le\mu_z,\qquad \Var[\dhat_z]\le 2^z d.$$
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$Y_z=\sum_{a\in D}X_a$ with $X_a=\mathbf 1[\zeros(h(a))\ge z]$ Bernoulli$(2^{-z})$ (Proposition \ref{prop:sample}). Linearity gives $\E[Y_z]=d2^{-z}$; the $X_a$ are pairwise independent, so Lemma \ref{lem:var} gives $\Var[Y_z]=d2^{-z}(1-2^{-z})$. Finally $\Var[\dhat_z]=4^z\Var[Y_z]\le4^z\cdot d2^{-z}=2^zd$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Chebyshev bound at a fixed level]\label{cor:cheb}
For every \emph{fixed} level $z$ and $\eps\in(0,1)$,
$$\Prb\bigl[\,|Y_z-\mu_z|>\eps\mu_z\,\bigr]\le\frac{\Var[Y_z]}{\eps^2\mu_z^2}\le\frac{1}{\eps^2\mu_z}.$$
\end{corollary}

**Design principle.** Corollary \ref{cor:cheb} shows that $\dhat_z$ is $\eps$-accurate with good probability as soon as $\mu_z\gtrsim1/\eps^2$. Memory is proportional to $Y_z$, so we want the largest $z$ (smallest sample) that still has $\mu_z\gtrsim1/\eps^2$. Since $d$ is unknown, so is this $z$. BJKST starts at $z=0$ and increases $z$ each time the buffer reaches the threshold $\tau=\Theta(1/\eps^2)$; because the samples are nested, this self-tuning costs nothing.

## The algorithm

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{BJKST, buffer-with-threshold, identifier-storing form}\label{alg:bjkst}
\small
\begin{tabbing}
\hspace{1.8em}\=\hspace{1.5em}\=\hspace{1.5em}\=\hspace{1.5em}\=\kill
\textbf{Require:} stream $a_1,\dots,a_m\in[n]$, $n=2^b$; accuracy $\eps\in(0,1)$ \\
1:\> $\tau\leftarrow\lceil c/\eps^2\rceil$ \hspace{1em} (c = 60 suffices; Theorem \ref{thm:accuracy}) \\
2:\> choose $h$ uniformly from the pairwise independent family of Lemma \ref{lem:gf} \\
3:\> $B\leftarrow\emptyset$, \ $z\leftarrow0$ \\
4:\> \textbf{for each} item $a$ of the stream \textbf{do} \\
5:\>\> \textbf{if} $\zeros(h(a))\ge z$ \textbf{then} \\
6:\>\>\> $B\leftarrow B\cup\{(a,\zeros(h(a)))\}$ \hspace{1em} ($B$ is a set: a repeated $a$ is a no-op) \\
7:\>\> \textbf{while} $|B|\ge\tau$ \textbf{do} \\
8:\>\>\> $z\leftarrow z+1$ \\
9:\>\>\> $B\leftarrow\{(x,\beta)\in B:\ \beta\ge z\}$ \\
10:\> \textbf{return} $\dhat=|B|\cdot2^z$
\end{tabbing}
\end{algorithm}

## Correctness invariant

\begin{lemma}[Invariant]\label{lem:inv}
Let $D_t$ be the set of distinct items among $a_1,\dots,a_t$. At all times during the processing of $a_t$, immediately after the insertion step and immediately after each pruning step, the buffer satisfies $B=\{(a,\zeros(h(a))):a\in D_t,\ \zeros(h(a))\ge z\}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction over the steps. Initially $B=\emptyset$, $z=0$, $D_0=\emptyset$. Insertion of $a_t$ adds its pair exactly when $\zeros(h(a_t))\ge z$; the pair is a function of $a_t$ alone, so re-inserting a repeated item changes nothing. Pruning from level $z$ to $z+1$ removes exactly the pairs with $\beta=z$, which is precisely the difference between the level-$z$ and level-$(z+1)$ sets. A pair removed at some level $z'$ has $\zeros<z'\le z$ for all later $z$, so it never qualifies for reinsertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Final state]\label{cor:final}
Let $Z$ denote the final value of $z$, with $Y_z=0$ for $z>b$. Then, deterministically, $|B|=Y_Z<\tau$ and $Y_z\ge\tau$ for all $z<Z$; that is, $Z=\min\{z\ge0:Y_z<\tau\}$, and the output is $\dhat=2^ZY_Z=\dhat_Z$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
After the last while-loop $|B|<\tau$, and by Lemma \ref{lem:inv} at the end of the stream $|B|=Y_Z$. For $z<Z$ the algorithm left level $z$ at some time $t$ because $|B|\ge\tau$; by the invariant $B$ then equalled $\{a\in D_t:\zeros(h(a))\ge z\}\subseteq S_z$, so $Y_z\ge\tau$.
\end{proof}

Corollary \ref{cor:final} is the key structural fact: the output is exactly the estimator $\dhat_z$ of the previous section evaluated at the \emph{random} level $Z$, the first level at which the full-stream sample falls below $\tau$. It also shows that $Z$ and the output depend only on $h$ and on the \emph{set} $D$, not on the order or multiplicities of the stream; this \evid{Literature}-derived consequence is tested empirically in Chapter \ref{ch:results} and is a unit-test target in Chapter \ref{ch:implementation}. The subtlety is that $Z$ is random, so Corollary \ref{cor:cheb} cannot be applied at $Z$ directly. The proof of the next theorem handles this with a union bound over the levels that can matter.

## Accuracy of a single copy

\begin{theorem}[Accuracy of one copy]\label{thm:accuracy}
Let $0<\eps<1$, $c=60$ and $\tau=\lceil c/\eps^2\rceil$. Then Algorithm \ref{alg:bjkst} outputs $\dhat$ with $\Prb[\,|\dhat-d|\le\eps d\,]\ge 5/6$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $\mu_z=d/2^z$. If $d<\tau/2$ then $Y_0=d<\tau$, so $z$ is never incremented, $Z=0$ and the output is exactly $d$. Assume $d\ge\tau/2$ and define the target level $z^*=\min\{z\ge0:\mu_z<\tau/2\}$. Since $\mu_b=d/n\le1<\tau/2$, we have $z^*\le b$. By minimality and halving, if $z^*\ge1$ then $\mu_{z^*-1}\ge\tau/2$, hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mustar}
\frac{\tau}{4}\le\mu_{z^*}<\frac{\tau}{2}.
\end{equation}
(The case $z^*=0$ would give $d=\mu_0<\tau/2$, excluded by assumption; so $z^*\ge1$ from now on.)

By Corollary \ref{cor:final} the output is wrong, i.e.\ $|2^ZY_Z-d|>\eps d$, only if $|Y_Z-\mu_Z|>\eps\mu_Z$ (multiply by $2^{-Z}$). Hence the failure event is contained in $E_1\cup E_2$, where
$$E_1=\{Z\ge z^*+1\},\qquad E_2=\{\exists z\le z^*:\ |Y_z-\mu_z|>\eps\mu_z\}.$$
Indeed, if $Z\le z^*$ and the output is wrong, take $z=Z$.

\emph{Bounding $E_1$ (level overshoots).} By Corollary \ref{cor:final}, $Z\ge z^*+1$ implies $Y_{z^*}\ge\tau$. Since $\mu_{z^*}<\tau/2$, this means $Y_{z^*}-\mu_{z^*}>\tau-\mu_{z^*}>\tau/2$. Chebyshev with $\Var[Y_{z^*}]\le\mu_{z^*}$ (Proposition \ref{prop:var}) gives
$$\Prb[E_1]\le\frac{\mu_{z^*}}{(\tau-\mu_{z^*})^2}\le\frac{\tau/2}{(\tau/2)^2}=\frac2\tau\le\frac2c,$$
where the middle inequality uses that $\mu\mapsto\mu/(\tau-\mu)^2$ is increasing on $(0,\tau)$, and the last uses $\tau\ge c/\eps^2\ge c$.

\emph{Bounding $E_2$ (bad concentration at low levels).} By a union bound and Corollary \ref{cor:cheb}, $\Prb[E_2]\le\sum_{z=0}^{z^*}1/(\eps^2\mu_z)$. Since $\mu_z=\mu_{z^*}2^{z^*-z}$, the sum is geometric:
$$\sum_{z=0}^{z^*}\frac{1}{\eps^2\mu_z}=\frac{1}{\eps^2\mu_{z^*}}\sum_{j=0}^{z^*}2^{-j}<\frac{2}{\eps^2\mu_{z^*}}\le\frac{8}{\eps^2\tau}\le\frac8c,$$
using \eqref{eq:mustar} and $\tau\ge c/\eps^2$.

\emph{Conclusion.} $\Prb[\text{fail}]\le\Prb[E_1]+\Prb[E_2]\le10/c=1/6$ for $c=60$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the argument is shaped this way]
The output is $\dhat_Z$ at a random level $Z$, so one cannot simply apply Chebyshev at $Z$. The proof (i) shows that $Z$ does not exceed the deterministic target $z^*$, where $\mu_{z^*}=\Theta(1/\eps^2)$, except with small probability, and (ii) takes a union bound of the level-wise Chebyshev failures over all levels $\le z^*$. Because $\mu_z$ doubles at each level moving down, the failure probabilities form a geometric series dominated by its last term, so the union bound costs only a constant factor. Only pairwise independence of $h$ was used.
\end{remark}

\begin{authornote}
(i) The parenthetical on $z^*=0$ in WP1 treats it as a trivial case with failure probability $0$; since $z^*=0$ contradicts $d\ge\tau/2$, the case cannot occur, and the text above says so. (ii) The constant $c=60$ is chosen to make $10/c=1/6$; it is a proof artefact, so the \emph{measured} failure frequency may be far below $1/6$, and measured errors should not be interpreted as ``violating'' or ``confirming'' the theorem unless this is taken into account. (iii) Re-check the constants $2/c$ and $8/c$ independently before the report is submitted; the arithmetic above reproduces WP1 and is consistent.
\end{authornote}

## Space complexity and update time {#sec:space}

### Identifier-storing form {-}

By Corollary \ref{cor:final} and the loop condition, $|B|<\tau$ at the end of each item's processing and $|B|\le\tau$ at all times. Each entry stores an identifier ($b=\log_2n$ bits) and a $\zeros$-value (at most $\lceil\log_2(b+1)\rceil$ bits); the counter $z$ needs $O(\log b)$ bits and $h$ needs $2\log_2n$ bits (Lemma \ref{lem:gf}). The total is
$$O\!\left(\frac{1}{\eps^2}\log n\right)\ \text{bits.}$$

### Fingerprint form {-}

The dominant cost is the identifiers. They can be replaced by short fingerprints: choose a second, independent 2-universal function $g:[n]\to[M]$ and store $(g(a),\zeros(h(a)))$ instead of $(a,\zeros(h(a)))$; duplicate detection is then done on fingerprints. The danger is a false collision, which makes a new item look like a duplicate and causes undercounting.

\begin{lemma}[Few items ever enter the buffer]\label{lem:few}
Let $I$ be the set of distinct items ever inserted into $B$ by the identifier-storing algorithm. Then, deterministically, $|I|\le\tau(b+1)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Insertions occur only at levels $0,\dots,b$ (no item has $\zeros>b$). At any level the buffer starts with fewer than $\tau$ elements, each insertion increases $|B|$ by one, and the level is left as soon as $|B|=\tau$; so at most $\tau$ insertions occur per level. A pruned item is never reinserted (Lemma \ref{lem:inv}), so no item is counted twice.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Space of the fingerprint form]\label{thm:fingerprint}
Take $M=\lceil10\tau^2(b+1)^2\rceil$. With $g$ independent of $h$, the fingerprint form outputs a $(1\pm\eps)$-approximation with probability at least $2/3$ and uses
$$O\!\left(\log n+\frac1{\eps^2}\Bigl(\log\frac1\eps+\log\log n\Bigr)\right)\ \text{bits.}$$
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Condition on $h$. While $g$ has no collision among the items of $I$, the fingerprint run is step-for-step identical to the identifier-storing run and has the same output. $I$ is determined by $h$ and the stream alone, and $g$ is independent of $h$, so by 2-universality and Lemma \ref{lem:few},
$$\Prb[\exists x\ne y\in I:g(x)=g(y)]\le\binom{|I|}{2}\frac1M\le\frac{\tau^2(b+1)^2}{2M}\le\frac1{20}.$$
With Theorem \ref{thm:accuracy}, the total failure probability is at most $\tfrac16+\tfrac1{20}=\tfrac{13}{60}<\tfrac13$. For space, each stored entry costs $\lceil\log_2M\rceil+\lceil\log_2(b+1)\rceil$ bits and $\log M=O(\log\tau+\log b)=O(\log\tfrac1\eps+\log\log n)$, so the buffer takes $O(\tau(\log\tfrac1\eps+\log\log n))$ bits; the two hash functions are described in $O(\log n)$ bits and $z$ takes $O(\log\log n)$ bits.
\end{proof}

The two space bounds must be kept apart: the identifier-storing form needs $\Theta(\tau\log n)$ bits for the buffer, the fingerprint form $O(\tau(\log\frac1\eps+\log\log n))$, at the price of an additional failure probability of $1/20$ and of the second hash function $g$.

\begin{authornote}
WP1, proof of the fingerprint theorem: (i) the step ``$M\le\mathrm{poly}(n)$'' used to bound the description of $g$ and $h$ by $O(\log n)$ bits holds only if $1/\eps\le\mathrm{poly}(n)$ (since $\tau=\Theta(1/\eps^2)$ enters $M$); (ii) the description length of a 2-universal $g$ into $[M]$ depends on the family chosen, which WP1 does not specify. Both points affect only the additive $O(\log n)$ term, but should be stated explicitly if the term is quoted.
\end{authornote}

### Update time {-}

Each item costs $O(1)$ hash evaluations (field operations in $\mathrm{GF}(2^b)$) and a dictionary lookup. Pruning rescans $B$ but is triggered at most $b+1$ times, and WP1 charges each level's scan to the at most $\tau$ insertions made at that level, giving $O(1)$ expected (amortised) time per item with a hash table.

\begin{authornote}
WP1, Section 8.3: a rescan at level $z$ touches up to $\tau$ stored entries even if few insertions occurred at that level, so the stated charging argument is only a sketch. What the argument does show is that total pruning work is $O((b+1)\tau)$, which is $O(1)$ per item only when $m=\Omega(\tau b)$. Also, one hash evaluation in $\mathrm{GF}(2^b)$ is $O(1)$ only in a word-RAM-style cost model where $b$-bit field multiplication counts as constant time. Treat the $O(1)$ amortised claim as \evid{Literature}/WP1 \emph{unverified} and check it against the measured runtime in Section \ref{sec:res-runtime}.
\end{authornote}

## Success-probability amplification (optional) {#sec:median}

The guarantees above are for a **single copy** with success probability at least $2/3$ (indeed $5/6$ for the identifier-storing form). Amplification is a separate, optional layer.

\begin{theorem}[Median trick]\label{thm:median}
Run $k=\lceil18\ln(1/\delta)\rceil$ independent copies (independent choices of $h$ and, where used, $g$) and output the median $\tilde d$ of their outputs. Then $\Prb[|\tilde d-d|\le\eps d]\ge1-\delta$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $W_j=1$ if copy $j$ is wrong. The $W_j$ are independent with $\Prb[W_j=1]\le1/3$, so $\E[W]\le k/3$ for $W=\sum_jW_j$. If fewer than $k/2$ copies are wrong, more than half the outputs lie in $[(1-\eps)d,(1+\eps)d]$, and so does their median. Hence the median fails only if $W\ge k/2$, and by Lemma \ref{lem:hoeff} with $t=k/6$, $\Prb[W\ge k/2]\le\Prb[W-\E W\ge k/6]\le\exp(-2(k/6)^2/k)=e^{-k/18}\le\delta$. The case $\Prb[W_j=1]<1/3$ is handled by stochastic domination.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Overall guarantee]\label{cor:overall}
There is a one-pass randomized streaming algorithm which, for any $\eps,\delta\in(0,1)$, outputs an $(\eps,\delta)$-approximation of $\Fzero$ using
$$O\!\left(\log\frac1\delta\cdot\Bigl(\log n+\frac1{\eps^2}\Bigl(\log\frac1\eps+\log\log n\Bigr)\Bigr)\right)\ \text{bits.}$$
\end{corollary}

## Context: related approaches and optimality

*Flajolet--Martin.* The trailing-zeros idea comes from Flajolet and Martin \cite{fm}, who track the maximum of $\zeros(h(a))$; that maximum is about $\log_2d$, giving a constant-factor estimate under idealised (fully random) hashing. Alon, Matias and Szegedy \cite{ams} showed that pairwise independent hashing suffices for a constant-factor approximation. BJKST keeps a *sample* of items rather than a single maximum, which is what buys $(1\pm\eps)$ accuracy under only pairwise independence.

*Minimum-value variant.* According to WP1, another presentation in \cite{bjkst} keeps the $t=\Theta(1/\eps^2)$ smallest hash values and estimates $d$ from the $t$-th smallest. Both are instances of ``sample by hash value, calibrate by the retention probability''. This variant is not analysed here and is not implemented unless stated in Chapter \ref{ch:implementation}.

*Optimality (context only).* Any randomized $(\eps,1/3)$-approximation of $\Fzero$ needs $\Omega(1/\eps^2)$ bits \cite{iw,wood} and $\Omega(\log n)$ bits; Kane, Nelson and Woodruff \cite{knw} gave an algorithm with $O(1/\eps^2+\log n)$ bits. By WP1, the fingerprint bound of Theorem \ref{thm:fingerprint} is within a $\log(1/\eps)+\log\log n$ factor of the $1/\eps^2$ term. This is cited only to help interpret the memory measured in Chapter \ref{ch:results}; we do not implement or evaluate the optimal algorithm.

## Summary of assumptions and limitations of the analysis

\begin{itemize}
\item The probabilities are over $h$ (and $g$) only; the stream is not adaptive to the random choices (A1). Guarantees are for a pairwise independent $h$ from the $\mathrm{GF}(2^b)$ family (A3); they say nothing about, e.g., a 64-bit mixing function used in practice.
\item The $5/6$ bound is for a single copy and is loose because of the constant $c=60$; $1-\delta$ requires the median construction.
\item The estimate is exact when $d<\tau/2$ (Theorem \ref{thm:accuracy}, first case), so differences between BJKST and exact counting only appear for larger $d$.
\item The identifier-storing space bound is not the fingerprint bound; they are not interchangeable.
\end{itemize}

## Unit tests and correctness validation

The invariants proved in Chapter \ref{ch:bjkst} translate directly into tests. The following are \evid{Future} until implemented; replace by actual test names and results.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Exactness for small $d$:} if $d<\tau/2$, the output equals $d$ (Theorem \ref{thm:accuracy}, first case).
\item \textbf{Duplicate insensitivity:} feeding each item any number of times and in any order does not change the output for a fixed $h$ (Corollary \ref{cor:final}).
\item \textbf{Invariant:} after every update, $B$ equals the set in Lemma \ref{lem:inv}, recomputed by brute force on small streams.
\item \textbf{Buffer bound:} $|B|<\tau$ after every update.
\item \textbf{Monotone level:} $z$ never decreases.
\item \textbf{Trailing-zeros function:} $\zeros(0)=b$ and agreement with a naive loop on small $b$.
\item \textbf{Hash family:} for small $b$, exhaustive enumeration of all $(a,c)$ confirms pairwise independence and $\Prb[\zeros\ge z]=2^{-z}$.
\item \textbf{Fingerprint form:} identical output to the identifier-storing form whenever no fingerprint collision occurs.
\end{enumerate}

# Experimental Methodology {#ch:methodology}

This chapter specifies the experiments. Unless stated otherwise, everything here is a \emph{proposal}; the status table below must be updated to show what was actually run, so that the report distinguishes designed from completed experiments.

## Research questions and hypotheses

The hypotheses below are \evid{Future} predictions derived from the theory; they are to be tested, not assumed. They hold for our implementation only to the extent that Section \ref{sec:assumption-check} is completed.

\begin{description}
\item[H1 (RQ1).] For $d\ge\tau/2$ the relative error is of order $\eps$ or smaller, and the fraction of trials with relative error $>\eps$ is at most $1/6$ (Theorem \ref{thm:accuracy}); it may be much smaller because $c=60$ is conservative. For $d<\tau/2$ the error is exactly $0$.
\item[H2 (RQ2).] The buffer size stays below $\tau=\lceil c/\eps^2\rceil$ and does not grow with $d$, while the exact set grows linearly in $d$.
\item[H3 (RQ3).] Per-item time of BJKST is roughly constant in stream length (Section \ref{sec:space}, subject to the caveat in the author note there).
\item[H4 (RQ4).] The output depends only on the set of distinct items and on $h$ (Corollary \ref{cor:final}); hence at equal $d$, error should not depend on frequencies or order.
\item[H5 (RQ5).] The error distribution across seeds is concentrated at scale $\eps$; the median of several copies reduces the tail.
\item[H6 (RQ6).] Hash functions that are not pairwise independent may match the pairwise independent family on benign streams but may differ on structured streams.
\end{description}

When one factor is varied, all others are held at the baseline values recorded in the configuration file (Appendix \ref{app:config}).

## Stream generators {#sec:generators}

All generators take $(n,m,\text{parameters},\text{seed})$ and return a stream over $[n]$; the true cardinality $d$ is always obtained from the exact baseline, never assumed from the generator's parameters.

\begin{description}
\item[Uniform.] Each $a_t$ is drawn independently and uniformly from $[n]$ (or from a pool of $u$ items). The resulting $d$ is random.
\item[High-duplication.] Choose $D_0\subseteq[n]$ with $|D_0|=d_0\ll m$ uniformly without replacement; the stream contains each item of $D_0$ once and the remaining $m-d_0$ positions are drawn uniformly from $D_0$; the order is then shuffled.
\item[High-cardinality.] A stream of $m$ items drawn without replacement, so that $d=m$ (every item distinct); requires $m\le n$.
\item[Skewed.] Items are ranked and item of rank $i$ is drawn with probability proportional to $i^{-s}$ (Zipf exponent $s>0$), from a pool of $u$ ranked items; $d$ is random and typically much smaller than $m$.
\end{description}

\begin{todobox}
Fix the numerical parameters ($n$, $m$, $d_0$, $u$, $s$) and justify each choice. Optionally add an \emph{ordering} factor (random, sorted, blocked) to test H4 directly.
\end{todobox}

## Algorithms and baselines

BJKST (identifier-storing form; fingerprint form and median of $k$ copies if implemented); the exact hash set; and, as an extension, HyperLogLog. HyperLogLog \placeholder{reference to be added; it is not in the source bibliography} is included only if implemented and tested, and is labelled as an extension wherever it appears.

## Metrics

For a trial with true cardinality $d$ and output $\dhat$:
$$\text{absolute error}=|\dhat-d|,\qquad \text{relative error}=\frac{|\dhat-d|}{d},\qquad \text{failure indicator}=\mathbf 1\bigl[\,|\dhat-d|>\eps d\,\bigr].$$
The empirical failure rate over $N$ independent trials estimates the failure probability of Definition \ref{def:approx} for the chosen $\eps$. Further metrics:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Runtime:} wall-clock time for processing the full stream, excluding stream generation, and derived time per item.
\item \textbf{Memory (two distinct measures, never mixed):} (a) \emph{logical sketch size}, the maximum $|B|$ reached and the bit count implied by the model of Section \ref{sec:space}; (b) \emph{measured peak process memory} from the operating system or language runtime, which includes overhead.
\item \textbf{Memory saving:} $1-M_{\mathrm{BJKST}}/M_{\mathrm{exact}}$, computed separately for each memory measure.
\end{itemize}

## Repeated trials and statistical summaries

Each configuration is run with $N=\placeholder{number}$ independent seeds. Summaries reported: mean, median, standard deviation and selected quantiles of the relative error; the empirical failure rate with a confidence interval (method to be stated, e.g.\ Wilson); and, for runtime and memory, medians with spread. The number of seeds must be large enough that the failure-rate interval is informative at the level being compared ($1/6$ for a single copy; $\delta$ for the median construction).

## Computing environment and measurement procedure

\begin{todobox}
Record hardware, operating system, runtime version, whether other processes were running, CPU frequency policy, warm-up runs, how peak memory is measured (and its resolution), and the number of repeated timings per configuration. Runtime and memory must be measured in a process that does not also hold the generated stream in memory unless the stream is common to all algorithms and this is stated.
\end{todobox}

## Reproducibility protocol

## Limitations and fair-comparison considerations

\begin{itemize}
\item Memory accounting must be matched: logical bits versus process bytes; compare algorithms at equal memory budget or equal target error, and say which.
\item Hash functions should be the same where possible, or the hashing cost reported separately.
\item Implementation language and data-structure overhead can dominate sketch size at small scales.
\item BJKST's guarantee is for pairwise independent hashing with constant $c=60$; HyperLogLog's guarantees are of a different kind (typically under fully random hashing), so error comparisons are empirical, not theoretical.
\item Runtime comparisons depend on the machine and on implementation quality; report both under the same procedure.
\end{itemize}

# Extended Derivations {#app:derivations}

\begin{todobox}
Include here only derivations that were shortened in the main text and that a reader may wish to check.
\end{todobox}

## Bookkeeping of the constant $c$ in Theorem \ref{thm:accuracy}

The failure probability is bounded by $\Prb[E_1]+\Prb[E_2]\le 2/c+8/c=10/c$. Requiring $10/c\le1/6$ gives $c\ge60$, which is the value used. For the fingerprint form the collision term $1/20$ is added, so the total is $1/6+1/20=13/60<1/3$. The choice $M=\lceil10\tau^2(b+1)^2\rceil$ makes $\tau^2(b+1)^2/(2M)\le1/20$. Smaller values of $c$ give a weaker proved bound ($10/c$ exceeds $1/6$) but may still perform well empirically; such experiments must be labelled accordingly.

## Why the median of independent copies need only $\Prb[W_j=1]\le1/3$

If each copy fails with probability $q_j\le1/3$, then $W=\sum_jW_j$ is stochastically dominated by a Binomial$(k,1/3)$ variable, so $\Prb[W\ge k/2]$ is at most the corresponding binomial tail, which Lemma \ref{lem:hoeff} bounds by $e^{-k/18}$. \placeholder{Add a formal coupling argument if required.}

# Additional Pseudocode and Implementation Notes {#app:pseudocode}

## Fingerprint form

This is a direct transcription of the description in Section \ref{sec:space}; it is not claimed to be identical to the pseudocode of \cite{bjkst}.

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{BJKST, fingerprint form (derived from the description in WP1)}\label{alg:fingerprint}
\small
\begin{tabbing}
\hspace{1.8em}\=\hspace{1.5em}\=\hspace{1.5em}\=\hspace{1.5em}\=\kill
\textbf{Require:} stream over $[n]$, $n=2^b$; $\eps\in(0,1)$ \\
1:\> $\tau\leftarrow\lceil60/\eps^2\rceil$, \ $M\leftarrow\lceil10\tau^2(b+1)^2\rceil$ \\
2:\> choose $h$ from the $\mathrm{GF}(2^b)$ family and an independent 2-universal $g:[n]\to[M]$ \\
3:\> $B\leftarrow\emptyset$, \ $z\leftarrow0$ \\
4:\> \textbf{for each} item $a$ \textbf{do} \\
5:\>\> \textbf{if} $\zeros(h(a))\ge z$ \textbf{then} $B\leftarrow B\cup\{(g(a),\zeros(h(a)))\}$ \\
6:\>\> \textbf{while} $|B|\ge\tau$ \textbf{do} $z\leftarrow z+1$; $B\leftarrow\{(x,\beta)\in B:\beta\ge z\}$ \\
7:\> \textbf{return} $|B|\cdot2^z$
\end{tabbing}
\end{algorithm}

\end{todobox}
